why_how.text: Before turning right across a cyclist in the lane, confirm the rider has yielded or passed, since bikes should pass left but often do not.
Bicycles are hard to see and need no daytime lights, unlike motorcycles.
Many young cyclists never trained or tested, so give children on bikes extra caution.
Share the road respectfully without honking, shouting or swerving at cyclists, which can startle them into a crash.
Night bicycles need a front white light visible at least five hundred feet ahead.
Rear red lights visible five hundred feet back are optional extras beside the mandatory rear reflectors.
Night bicycles need reflective sidewalls or spoke reflectors on both wheels, with spoke units near the rim and visible both sides in the stated colors.
Bicycle brakes must be strong enough to skid the wheels on dry, level, clean pavement.
A fluorescent orange flag six feet above the road is encouraged for visibility from behind.
Treat bicycles as vehicles, watching entries, bikeways, sidewalks, turns and children darting between parked cars.
Park clear of travel lanes and visible to approaching traffic from both directions.
Use marked areas, set the brake, and leave a manual in gear or an automatic in park.
Check traffic before opening doors, exit curbside when possible, and close doors promptly.
Never leave keys inside; lock up whenever leaving the vehicle.
On roadways park as far from traffic as possible, hugging the curb or the shoulder edge.
The vehicle must sit within eighteen inches of the curb or shoulder edge.
Night front bicycle lights are mandatory white, while rear red lights are optional extras beside the mandatory rear reflectors.
Spoke reflectors sit near the rim in white or amber at the front wheel and amber or red at the rear, while sidewall reflection covers the tire sides.
A right turn across a cyclist waits for the rider to yield or pass, while a cyclist should pass motorists on the left.
Trained riders are expected to know the rules, while untrained young riders demand extra caution from drivers.
A parked car must clear travel lanes and stay visible both ways, while a roadway park hugs the curb or shoulder edge.

Never park where construction blockage results, or within thirty feet of a signal, stop sign or yield sign.
Keep fifteen feet from fire hydrants and fifty feet from railroad crossings.
Stay within eighteen inches of the curb and clear of fire-station driveways by twenty feet same-side or seventy-five across.
Never block driveways, alleys, private roads or curb cuts for sidewalk access.
Never park on a bridge, elevated structure, tunnel or underpass.
Never park on the wrong side, alongside another parked vehicle, or on railroad tracks.
Never park where a sign forbids it or in a marked accessible space without a permit; violations draw fines.
White curbs serve passenger stops and yellow curbs attended loading, while red curbs ban every stop.
Hydrants need fifteen feet and crossings fifty, while signals and signs need thirty and intersection crosswalks twenty.
Same-side fire driveways need twenty feet clear, while opposite-side driveways need seventy-five.

why_how.text: Liability insurance is mandatory except for motorcycles, at twenty-five thousand per person, fifty thousand per accident, and ten thousand for the property of others.
Stopped or crashed motorists show insurance evidence to officers with license and registration, and evidence rides in the vehicle always.
Uninsured driving is a misdemeanor: a first offense draws at least two hundred fifty up to five hundred dollars, up to ten days in jail, or both, plus five record points.

Repeat uninsured driving draws at least three hundred fifty dollars or up to ten days in jail, with plate and registration suspension for ninety days, or one hundred eighty for a third or later offense.
Crash responsibility without payment within sixty days suspends license and registration automatically until payment or six years pass, plus fresh insurance evidence.
Owners of more than twenty-five Montana-registered vehicles may qualify as self-insurers.
Non-residents face the same responsibility law on adequate in-state policies, losing Montana driving privileges for noncompliance with notice to their home state.
The insurance verification system matches registration and insurer data so officers, courts, licensing offices and the public can confirm coverage in real time.
Minimum coverage splits per person, per accident and for property, while evidence must ride along in the vehicle always.
A first uninsured offense draws fine or jail plus points, while repeat offenses add plate and registration suspension.
Self-insurer status fits large fleets, while non-residents rely on adequate in-state policies or lose privileges.
